title: 1:30 AM on November 3, 2024 happens twice in New York, and fold picks which one
assumption: A local wall-clock time plus a timezone name uniquely identifies one instant.

input.description: Log timestamps, scheduled job times, or user-entered times that fall in the one-hour window a clock repeats when a timezone falls back off DST.

what_goes_wrong: Two events both logged as '2024-11-03 01:30 America/New_York' can be a full hour apart in real time, and nothing about the string itself says which.
why: On 2024-11-03 the America/New_York clock reaches 01:59:59 EDT, then repeats back to 01:00:00, now as EST, before continuing to 02:00. The wall-clock hour 01:00-01:59 therefore occurs twice, at two different UTC instants one hour apart. PEP 495 (Python 3.6) added a `fold` attribute to Python's datetime specifically for this: fold=0 (the default) means 'the first occurrence' (-04:00, EDT), fold=1 means 'the second occurrence' (-05:00, EST). Two systems that both construct 01:30 without agreeing on fold silently disagree by exactly one hour.

repros.code:
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo
from datetime import datetime

tz = ZoneInfo("America/New_York")
first = datetime(2024, 11, 3, 1, 30, tzinfo=tz, fold=0)
second = datetime(2024, 11, 3, 1, 30, tzinfo=tz, fold=1)
print(first.utcoffset(), second.utcoffset())
print(first.astimezone(ZoneInfo("UTC")))
print(second.astimezone(ZoneInfo("UTC")))

fix: Store instants in UTC, never a bare local wall-clock string, especially around DST transitions. If you must accept or log an ambiguous local time, record the UTC offset or the fold/occurrence alongside it, not just the wall-clock string.
